newsitem.title: USA: US Rep. says FCC chief should consider quitting.
newsitem.headline: US Rep. says FCC chief should consider quitting.

text.p: A key lawmaker who helped rewrite the nation's communications laws suggested Tuesday that Federal Communications Commission chairman Reed Hundt should consider quitting.

Rep. Jack Fields, the outgoing head of the House telecommunications and finance subcommittee, accused Hundt of not following the intent of Congress in implementing the communications act enacted in February.
"To see one person come in and try and rewrite the legislation is absolutely abhorrent," the Texas Republican said of Hundt in an interview with Reuters.

"He would serve his own intersts well if he would find something else to do," said Fields, predicting Hundt would face rough sledding from Congress in 1997 and ultimately would "become an embarrassment to the president."

In particular, Fields cited the FCC's "interconnection" order for opening the $100 billion local phone market to competition. A U.S. appeals court last month suspended key provisions of the order, which has been challenged by local phone companies and state regulators.

The FCC approved the interconnection order unanimously in August. It spells out how long-distance companies and other new entrants to the local phone business can hook up to the local network. In particular, it spells out the prices that new entrants should pay local carriers for the linkup.
"We certainly never envisioned a federal pricing structure," said Fields.

Earlier, in a speech to state regulators in San Francisco, Fields said that if Hundt had made an "honest mistake" in implementing the communications law, "I pledge to work with him in my remaining months to write regulations consistent with the intent of Congress."

But he added: "If the interconnection order is not a simple and honest mistake and Chairman Hundt was 'willful' and 'intentionally disregarded' the specific language of the act and the intent of Congress, then he should step aside -- he should resign or the president should appoint someone else ...."
An FCC official declined to comment.
